Open source · for people who shoot

yiibu一步

A folder of phone clips, one step to a vertical short you can post.

All four shipped. These are silent excerpts.

It picks the shots, orders them, writes the captions, lines them up with the audio, lays in music, builds the cover — and then tells you the plan before it cuts anything. What you type is this: 

edit video ~/Downloads/what-i-shot

No flags, no config file. The word yiibu does not have to appear. Everything else it either asks you or decides itself.

Same folder, two roads

Say you went to an event and came home with forty-odd clips.

You do it

  • Watch forty-odd clips end to end, pick the ones worth using
  • Type the captions, line each one up by hand
  • Find music, manually duck it wherever somebody talks
  • Build a cover, export, export a second time without music
  • Quality tracks how careful you are, and what hour you are on

It does it

  • You pick nothing. Choosing shots and ordering them is the job
  • Your words land on their own timings, keywords turn gold
  • Music sits underneath and steps out of the way of speech
  • Three files, handed over at once
  • 20 checks, and it will not hand over until they pass. Tiredness does not enter into it
What you get Three files at the top of the folder: a music version, a no-music version, a cover image. The no-music one is not a bonus — it is the instrument. Subtract it from the music version and you can measure whether the bed actually stepped out of the way.
What it needs A folder. That is the only thing it cannot proceed without. Length, template and music all have defaults, and it reads them out before cutting, so vetoing any line takes one reply.
What it will not do It will not shoot for you. It will not decide what may be published — footage that looks like a session gets you a question first. And it will not say "done": when everything passes, it says "it passes the checks".

Getting started

Install it, then say one sentence

If you use Claude Code

/plugin marketplace add chyiiiiiiiiiiii/yiibu
/plugin install yiibu

If you use anything else (Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, or a person)

git clone https://github.com/chyiiiiiiiiiiii/yiibu
cd yiibu && ./install.sh

The whole standard lives in an AGENTS.md at the repo root, and every rule in it is a command you can run rather than advice you have to remember. Swap the tool, the model, or the person, and the same checks still run. That is the point of writing it that way.

Then

edit video ~/Downloads/what-i-shot

It needs very little: ffmpeg, Pillow, numpy. The caption font is bundled. Speech captions, B-roll and music are optional — when a piece is missing that feature skips cleanly. It never errors on absence.

Four things worth doing while you shoot

  • One folder per video, untrimmed. Put everything in. Selecting is its job, and the clips you trim by hand tend to lose the half-sentence a caption needed.
  • Shoot vertical. Rotation is read per clip, so a mixed folder survives, but a native vertical shot always beats a cropped landscape one.
  • Fluff a line? Clap once, then say it again. A clap deletes the 3 seconds before it, so the bad take never reaches the edit.
  • Shoot the opening and the ending on purpose. The first 2 seconds decide whether anyone stays; the last shot is the payoff. One deliberately strange image and one deliberate closer give the edit both ends.

One more: get the phone close when you speak. Speech below a certain level carries no words a caption can quote. One sentence said near the mic beats three distant retakes.

That is what it is. Here is the other half

Why it can hold that bar

Five short rounds, and each one asks you first — not to test you, but because the second you find out you bet wrong is the only second any of this stays in your head. About ten minutes. Every question is answerable from common sense; none of it needs a technical background.

All right, start Skip it, show me the six takeaways
00

The music drops out in the last two seconds

You have finished a 90-second short. You have watched it: picture, captions, cover, all good.

On the way out you notice the music is inaudible for the final two seconds. You check why: that is the song's own outro, which was always going to fade. Nothing is broken.

Do you ship it?

This is exactly how it shipped broken, twice. The line is: the ending may not fall below −32. Both times the measurement came back −34. Both times it was measured, seen, and then talked away — first as "that's the song's own outro", then as "that's the tail fade". Both explanations were true. Both went out. Both times what a viewer heard was the sound falling off a cliff at the end. Your call there was not stupid. It is just how people work: being able to explain a number feels like having checked it.
Yes, and this is the one rule in the project that outranks every number in it. It does not claim the explanation is wrong. It claims that explaining and checking are two different acts, and in the moment a person only performs one of them.
This is the move it guards against hardest. A line that gets loosened is a line that does not exist — relax it for this video and the next one will need more room again. Thresholds can move: this project shifted its own caption pill from 23% of frame height to 18%. What made that healthy is that the change was written down — who asked, what day, and why. An adjustment nobody recorded is indistinguishable from switching the check off.

The rule reads like this, word for word:

Do not reason about whether a measurement is acceptable.
A number outside the threshold is a failure even when you can explain it.

TakeawayExplaining a number is not checking it.

01

The code that refuses to hand over

Yours

Its answer

Almost always somewhere measurable and invisible. The music at the end has already stopped. One caption is on screen for 0.75 seconds and nobody can finish reading it. The cover was built from a landscape frame — right shape, picture on its side. The editor spent the whole session staring at the picture, and none of that waves at you.

So it wrote down what "finished" means as 20 measurable things. None of them is a rule somebody imagined. Each one is a mistake that actually shipped once, turned afterwards into code.

Here are the 19. Flip a switch to "broken" and see whether it holds.

Music at the end
Caption dwell
Caption type
Cover
Shot length
Your decisions written down
0red
0exit code
—result

    The three exit codes mean three things, and it has to report them that way:

    • 0  shippable. It says "it passes the checks". It does not say "finished".
    • 1  something is broken. What is broken is the video, so the next move is to fix the video, never the threshold.
    • 2  nothing is broken, but some checks were deferred by a choice you recorded. It has to say out loud that this is not finished, and which parts are outstanding.

    Why go to that trouble? Because the same mistakes were written into documentation twice in this project's history, and came back both times. They stopped only once a piece of code refused to continue. Documentation is read by people, and people read it and forget. The checks do not.

    There are also 372 tests whose only job is to confirm those 20 checks still catch the original mistakes. Without that layer, checks rot quietly into always-pass.

    TakeawayQuality cannot live in remembering. The code that blocks you is the standard.

    02

    Twenty minutes of footage. How long should the video be?

    You went to an event. Forty-odd clips, twenty minutes total. You are posting one vertical short.

    This is the intuitive arithmetic: footage divided by shot length. The problem is not that it cuts too little, it is that it points the wrong way — it makes the video as long as the material allows rather than as long as the content can carry. Shoot 20 minutes, get 3; shoot 5, get 45 seconds. The same event turns into different videos because you hit record more times. What a viewer feels is not "rich material", it is a long stretch where nothing happens.
    Right. Length is additive, not a division. Count the things worth a moment of their own, add them up one at a time, and whatever that comes to is the length.
    A ceiling is a limit, not a target. Pin the length first and the work turns into filling time, and there is only one way to fill time: put in the things that were not worth watching. This is also why naming a duration in your request tends to make the result worse, which the next round covers.

    3s opening + 4 payloads of 11s + 11s connective + 5s ending = 63s

    Of those four numbers only one — how many things are worth a moment — is your judgement. The other three have measured ranges behind them, taken from one edit the author reviewed and accepted: 39 segments, 2:02. The platform ranges are labelled as conventions, because there is no trustworthy retention data for them and the project did not invent any to sound authoritative.

    One more thing worth keeping: when it feels long, cut the connective tissue, never the payloads. Connective tissue is walking in, the room, somebody laughing. It makes the video flow, and removing it costs you nothing you were trying to say.

    As for the first shot, the rule is one line: put the strangest image in the folder there. Not the sign, not walking in. If the strangest image is at 4:51 of a five-minute clip, that is frame one.

    TakeawayLength is added up, not divided down.

    03

    What you should actually tell it

    The following is real. A food video that has since been published — the author did not type, they talked, and dropped the music in as an attachment:

    Please help me shorten the video. This video is mainly a food sharing session. I brought friends from Singapore and Hong Kong to this very authentic Taipei lamb hot pot restaurant, "Mo Zai Yang." Even at lunchtime, it was still very crowded. […] I filmed many close-ups of the food and also captured everyone's reactions while eating. […]

    1. Subtitles: identify and display subtitles naturally for parts with dialogue. Remember to add both Chinese and English subtitles.
    2. Music and Atmosphere: use music (you know there will be some ducking) to enhance the atmosphere […]
    3. Cover and Ending: that's up to you to decide.

    Exactly three things in there changed the edit: the restaurant is called Mo Zai Yang, the friends came from Singapore and Hong Kong, and the music file. Every other line changed nothing at all, and that is fine.

    Those three have one thing in common: the footage cannot supply them. No frame spells out "Mo Zai Yang", and no pixel says where anyone flew in from.

    Your turn. Rank these four, most worth saying at the top, least worth saying at the bottom.

    The top kind is a boundary: which slide must not be zoomed into, who should not appear, which shot has to stay. No amount of footage analysis will find these, because they are not in the footage. They are in your memory.

    The bottom kind is what it works out anyway. Pinning the length has a side effect too: the job turns from "cut what is not worth watching" into "reach 60 seconds".

    So the rule is not "more context is better". It is: say what the footage cannot say.

    There is exactly one thing it will stop dead for: a missing footage folder.

    Everything else it only asks when you are the only one who could know, and it asks in one batch rather than one question at a time: a fact on screen it cannot read (you were there, it was not), whether a stretch may be published, or filenames that contradict their contents. The rest it decides, then reads the decisions back to you.

    TakeawaySay what the footage cannot say. Let it measure the rest.

    04

    Would you tidy up that caption?

    Speech recognition turns the audio into text, and one line comes back as "the broth is made from lamb bone". You listen twice and it sounds more like "the broth is, uh, made from lamb leg bones, y'know" — which is also wordier and reads worse.

    Yours

    Its answer

    The one you heard, not a word changed. A caption sitting under someone speaking is a set of quotation marks; tidying the sentence puts words in their mouth that they did not say. Anything you genuinely cannot confirm leaves the quoted layer entirely — it becomes a note you wrote, in a different style and size, so the viewer can see it is commentary rather than a quote.

    This sounds small, and it is the one rule written at the very front of the project that code cannot fully enforce. A machine can only check whether those words are in the audio underneath: a first word cut off, a line more than a second late, a sentence sitting over the wrong shot — all blocked. Whether a line was tidied up, it cannot see, because the tidied version sounds better.

    Transcription has two traps, and both produce captions that sound completely normal, so it verifies before writing any:

    • Your prompt comes back as the transcript. On noisy audio, speech recognition hands you the hint you gave it as though it heard it, at ordinary-looking confidence. That becomes a quote the person never said, sitting on their face. Hence the rule: do not give it a prompt.
    • The loop. On near-silent audio one phrase repeats forever.

    Somewhere loud enough — a restaurant at lunchtime — the honest move is not to quote at all. The captions on that food video above are written by a person, not transcribed, because nothing that came back from that room was trustworthy. That was a decision, and it is on the record.

    TakeawayA quote is word for word. Tidying it is fabrication.

    05

    All 20 green. Can you hand it over?

    The run finishes. Every check passes, exit code 0.

    This is the most expensive thing to believe. It happened: an event video passed all 12 checks that existed at the time while three of six teams got two shots each and the other three got four. No check goes red for that, because it is not a defect. It is leaving somebody out. Checks have eyes for "something is broken". They have none for "something is missing".
    Right, and it is required to phrase it that way. It may say "it passes the checks" and may not say "finished" until a person has actually watched the thing.
    Ten more checks would not touch it. This is not a question of how tight the thresholds are, it is a question of kind: checks measure whether something is broken. They cannot measure whether it is true, and they cannot measure who got left out. Adding more only makes passing look more trustworthy, which is the wrong direction.
    —checks
    —gap

    So it does one more thing: it prints a table of who got how many seconds, right under the check report. That table grades nothing and will never block you, because how much time a subject deserves is a judgement, not a threshold — and a threshold would only get argued down until it passed. Its whole job is to make not looking difficult.

    The other blind spot is worse: what may be published. A 93.6-second event recap went out with every check green, and 41 of those seconds were under an embargo. Nothing in the pixels could have told a machine that. So now it scans the material before any cutting and asks you one question when the footage looks like conference sessions. Food, running and family clips trip nothing, and you are never bothered.

    TakeawayAll green means you missed the known landmines. Nothing more.

    Apply it

    What have you got in that folder?

    Pick one and see how it gets handled, and the one sentence worth adding.

    It uses—
    Location audio—

    Likely to block you—

    Retrieval

    No hints. Same points, asked differently

    One

    You change the threshold from −32 to −35 and the video passes. Is that solved?

    After that change, this line never stops you again. The thing it was there to catch — sound falling off a cliff at the end — has not gone anywhere. It has just become something you have to remember, and remembering is the exact failure this whole page is about.
    Right. The difference is whether it leaves a trace. Loosening a line is not the crime. Loosening it where nobody can see is.
    Too rigid — thresholds do move. This project shifted its own caption pill from 23% of frame height to 18%. What made that change healthy is that who asked, what day, and why went into the spec file alongside it, and it became the default for every video after.

    Two

    Yours

    Its answer

    One, truth: a caption perfectly placed and perfectly timed that says something nobody said, or a number no slide shows. Two, omission: half the people in the room got two shots and the rest got four. Neither is a fault, so neither is measurable.

    Three

    Which of these carries no information at all for this particular edit?

    B. There is a quick test for this: move the sentence onto any other video. Does it still hold? "Make it look good" holds for every video ever made, which is how you know it says nothing about this one. A is a fact absent from the frame and C is a boundary only you know — move either onto a different video and it goes wrong immediately, which is the proof that they carry something.

    Six to take with you

    What you should still have next week

    Explaining is not checking Past the line is a failure however good the reason. Being able to explain it is not having checked it.
    Quality cannot live in remembering The code that blocks you is the standard. Rules kept in a document broke twice here.
    Length is added up Opening plus the things worth a moment plus connective plus ending. Not footage divided by shot length. When it drags, cut connective.
    Say what the footage cannot The name of the place, who must not appear, the shot that has to stay. Length and music it works out better than you.
    A quote is word for word Tidying a sentence puts words in someone's mouth. If you are unsure, make it a note you wrote instead.
    All green is not good It means you missed the known landmines. Truth, and who got left out, still need a person to watch.
